messages.subject: compilation crashes R with large dataset
messages.subject_clean: compilation crashes R with large dataset
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

First, I want to say thank you for all the help you've provided thus far with nimble - I really appreciate it. Your suggestions have made my model run considerably faster!

Second, I'm currently having an issue with compilation when I expand my model to include more data. The code below works for a small number of timesteps (t = 4; 336 observations, 31 columns) and quickly gets through every phase of building and running the model. I'd like to eventually run the model on around 360 timesteps (~30k observations, 31 columns). As an intermediate step to determine how long it would take to run the full model, I wanted to first test it on a third of the data. Every step through buildMCMC works, and then compilation runs for a bit and crashes. nimbleModel took 5.5 sec, configureMCMC took < 1 sec, and buildMCMC took ~ 55 minutes. However, compilation does not complete and instead crashes R.

I'm doing all of this through google cloud computing, so initially, I ran this on a VM with 64gb memory. When compilation approached ~ 64gb usage of memory, it crashed, so I figured I'd expand the VM to 128gb and try again. R again crashed at ~ 125gb of memory. If this truly is a memory problem, I'm happy to keep expanding the memory, but I'm hoping there's another way to do this! Any suggestions on what to do?

Steps I've taken to speed up the model and get this to work include leaving my design matrix in R and vectorizing beta to reduce the nodes from ~5000 to 168 multivariate elements. For reference, here is what the current configuration with a third of the data looks like:

===== Monitors =====
thin = 1: alpha, eta, sigma_phi, beta_param, tau
===== Samplers =====
RW_block sampler (168)
  - beta[]  (168 multivariate elements)
RW sampler (10)
  - alpha[]  (2 elements)
  - eta[]  (2 elements)
  - sigma_phi[]  (2 elements)
  - beta_param[]  (2 elements)
  - tau[]  (2 elements)
CAR_normal sampler (240)
  - phi_sp[]  (240 multivariate elements)
   user  system elapsed
  0.807   0.000   0.805

## code to keep X out of nimble model and vectorize betas -------
makeRfuns <- function(array_of_matrices) {
  x <- array_of_matrices
  RcalcXB <- function(beta) {
    XB <- array(NA, dim=c(s, t))
    for(m in 1:t) {
      for(j in 1:s) {
        XB[j, m] <- (x[j,1:p,m] %*% beta[j,1:p])[1,1]
      }
    }
    return(XB)
  }
  cov_matrix <- function(beta_param) {
    m <- matrix(NA, 5, 5)
    diag(m) <- rep(1,5)
    m[upper.tri(m, diag = FALSE)] <- c(beta_param, beta_param^2, beta_param,
                                       beta_param^3, beta_param^2, beta_param,
                                       beta_param^4, beta_param^3, beta_param^2, beta_param)
    kron <- as.matrix(kronecker(diag(6), forceSymmetric(m)))
    addrow <- rbind(rep(0,30), kron)
    return(matrix(cbind(c(1,rep(0,30)), addrow), 31, 31))
  }
  list(RcalcXB = RcalcXB, cov_matrix = cov_matrix)
}

# Create the functions and put them in .GlobalEnv
Rfuns <- makeRfuns(X_array)
RcalcXB_int <- Rfuns$RcalcXB
cov_mat_int <- Rfuns$cov_matrix

## Define the nimbleRcall nimbleFunctions to call the R function
RcalcXB_model <- nimbleRcall(function(beta = double(2)) {},
                             returnType = double(2), Rfun = 'RcalcXB_int')
cov_mat_model <- nimbleRcall(function(beta_param = double()) {},
                             returnType = double(2), Rfun = 'cov_mat_int')

## nimble code --------
ZIPcode_icar <- nimbleCode({
  # params for mu and pi calculations
  # i = 2 -> one for mu and one for pi
  for(i in 1:2) {
    alpha[i] ~ dnorm(0,5) # scalar intercept params
    eta[i] ~ dbeta(8,2) # AR param for spatio-temporal adjustments
    sigma_phi[i] ~ dnorm(0,1)  # time difference spatial sd
    beta_param[i] ~ dunif(0,1) # AR param for betas
    tau[i] ~ dnorm(0,5) # precision param
  }

  # AR(1) on betas - for overfitting (one set of betas for each of 84 regions)
  zeros[1:p] <- rep(0,p)
  for(i in 1:2) {
    cov_matrix[1:p, 1:p, i] <- cov_mat_model(beta_param[i]) * beta_sd
    for(j in 1:s) {
      beta[j, 1:p, i] ~ dmnorm(zeros[1:p], cov = cov_matrix[1:p, 1:p, i])
    }
  }

  # spatio-temporal effects
  for(i in 1:2) {
    phi_sp[1:s, 1, i] ~ dcar_normal(adj = adj[1:L], weights = weights[1:L], num = num[1:s], tau = tau[i])
    phi_full[1:s, 1, i] <- phi_sp[1:s, 1, i] * sigma_phi[i]
    for(m in 2:t) {
      phi_sp[1:s, m, i] ~ dcar_normal(adj = adj[1:L], weights = weights[1:L], num = num[1:s], tau = tau[i])
      phi_full[1:s, m, i] <- eta[i] * phi_full[1:s, m-1, i]  + phi_sp[1:s, m, i] * sigma_phi[i]
    }
  }

  # likelihood params and calculations
  XB_mu[1:s, 1:t] <- RcalcXB_model(beta[1:s, 1:p, 1])
  XB_pi[1:s, 1:t] <- RcalcXB_model(beta[1:s, 1:p, 2])
  for(m in 1:t) {
    for(j in 1:s) {
      log(u[j, m]) <- alpha[1] + XB_mu[j, m] + phi_full[j, m, 1] + log_area[j]
      logit(pi_param[j, m]) <- alpha[2] + XB_pi[j, m] + phi_full[j, m, 2]
    }
  }

  # vectorize mu and pi
  mu[1:(s*t)] <- nimC(u[1:s,1:t])
  pi[1:(s*t)] <- nimC(pi_param[1:s,1:t])

  for(q in 1:(s*t)) {
    y[q] ~ dZIP(mu[q], zeroProb = pi[q])
  }
})

# define model
# data, constants, inits
constants <- list(s = s, p = p, t = t, adj = nbInfo$adj, weights = nbInfo$weights,
                  num = nbInfo$num, log_area = log_area, L = length(nbInfo$adj), beta_sd = 0.01)
data <- list(y = y)
inits <- list(phi_sp = array(matrix(rnorm(s*t, 0, 1), nrow = s, ncol = t), dim = c(s, t, 2)),
              alpha = c(0.5, 0.5), beta = array(matrix(rnorm(s*p, 0, 1), s,p), dim = c(s,p, 2)),
              eta = c(0.5, 0.5), beta_param = c(0.5, 0.5), tau = c(0.5, 0.5),
              sigma_phi = c(0.5, 0.5), cov_matrix = array(matrix(rnorm(p*p, 0, 1), p, p), dim = c(p, p, 2)),
              zeros = rep(0.5,p)) #,
              #lifted_chol_oPcov_matrix_oB1to31_comma_1to31_comma_i_cB_cP_L11 = array(matrix(rnorm(p*p, 0, 0.1),p,p), dim = c(2, p,p)))

system.time(ZIP_mod_icar <- nimbleModel(ZIPcode_icar, constants = constants, data = data, inits = inits, calculate = FALSE))

## configure, build MCMC and compile -------
system.time(zip_conf_icar <- configureMCMC(ZIP_mod_icar, useConjugacy = FALSE))
zip_conf_icar$addMonitors("u", "pi_param", "mu", "pi", "phi_full", "beta")

system.time(zip_mcmc_icar <- buildMCMC(zip_conf_icar))

system.time(comp_zip_mcmc_icar <- compileNimble(ZIP_mod_icar, zip_mcmc_icar, resetFunctions = TRUE))

Thank you in advance for your help!

best,
Liz

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I adapted some JAGS code for a community N-mixture model from section 11.10 of Kery and Royle's AHM book, volume 1 for a multispecies count dataset. I also included a beta-binomial specification for estimating imperfect species detection. In the future, I would also like to incorporate a conditional autoregressive process to account for spatial correlations between survey locations. However, I have had considerable trouble with trying to fit some test models.

In brief, while running nimbleMCMC() on my nimbleModel, I have been getting some of the following errors, depending on whether I use flat dgamma() or dunif() priors on variance-related parameters involved:

Monitored nodes are valid for WAIC
compiling... this may take a minute. Use 'showCompilerOutput = TRUE' to see C++ compilation details.
compilation finished.
runMCMC's handling of nburnin changed in nimble version 0.6-11. Previously, nburnin samples were discarded *post-thinning*.  Now nburnin samples are discarded *pre-thinning*.  The number of samples returned will be floor((niter-nburnin)/thin).
running chain 1...
Warning: R object of different size than NimArrDouble. R obj has size 14 but NimArrDbl has size 35.
Warning: R object of different size than NimArrDouble. R obj has size 1 but NimArrDbl has size 2.
Warning: R object of different size than NimArrDouble. R obj has size 1 but NimArrDbl has size 5.
|-------------|-------------|-------------|-------------|
|-------------------------------------------------------|
Error in quantile.default(x, 0.025) :
  missing values and NaN's not allowed if 'na.rm' is FALSE

or

Monitored nodes are valid for WAIC
compiling... this may take a minute. Use 'showCompilerOutput = TRUE' to see C++ compilation details.
compilation finished.
runMCMC's handling of nburnin changed in nimble version 0.6-11. Previously, nburnin samples were discarded *post-thinning*.  Now nburnin samples are discarded *pre-thinning*.  The number of samples returned will be floor((niter-nburnin)/thin).
running chain 1...
Warning: R object of different size than NimArrDouble. R obj has size 14 but NimArrDbl has size 35.
Warning: R object of different size than NimArrDouble. R obj has size 1 but NimArrDbl has size 2.
Warning: R object of different size than NimArrDouble. R obj has size 1 but NimArrDbl has size 5.
warning: problem initializing stochastic node a[1, 1]: logProb is -Inf.
... etc ...
|-------------|-------------|-------------|-------------|
|-------------------------------------------------------|
Error in quantile.default(x, 0.025) :
  missing values and NaN's not allowed if 'na.rm' is FALSE

Here's one of my test models:

code100 <- nimbleCode({

    # Community priors (with hyperparameters) for species-specific parameters
    for(k in 1:nspec){
        phi[k] ~ dunif(0, 1)                                   # Zero-inflation
        alpha0[k] ~ dnorm(mu.alpha0L, tau=tau.alpha0)          # Detection intercepts
        beta0[k] ~ dnorm(mu.beta0, tau=tau.beta0)              # Abundance intercepts
    for(v in 1:npred){
        beta[k, v] ~ dnorm(mu.beta[v], tau=tau.beta[v])        # Slopes abundance
    }
    for(v in 1:ndet){
        alpha[k, v] ~ dnorm(mu.alpha[v], tau=tau.alpha[v])     # Slopes detection
     }
    }

    # Hyperpriors for community hyperparameters
    # Abundance model
    mu.beta0 ~ dunif(-5, 5)
    tau.beta0 <- pow(sd.beta0, -2)
    sd.beta0 ~ dunif(0, 5)
    for(v in 1:npred){
        mu.beta[v] ~ dunif(-5, 5)
        tau.beta[v] <- pow(sd.beta[v], -2)
    }
    sd.beta[1] ~ dunif(0, 5)
    sd.beta[2] ~ dunif(0, 5)
    sd.beta[3] ~ dunif(0, 5)
    sd.beta[4] ~ dunif(0, 5)
    sd.beta[5] ~ dunif(0, 5)

    # Detection model
    mu.alpha0L <- logit(mu.alpha0)
    mu.alpha0 ~ dunif(0, 0.1)
    tau.alpha0 <- pow(sd.alpha0, -2)
    sd.alpha0 ~ dunif(0, 1)
    for(v in 1:ndet){
        mu.alpha[v] ~ dunif(0, 0.1)
        tau.alpha[v] <- pow(sd.alpha[v], -2)
    }
    sd.alpha[1] ~ dunif(0, 1)
    sd.alpha[2] ~ dunif(0, 1)

    #Beta-binomial specification
    tau <- exp(tau.log)
    tau.log ~ dnorm(0, sd=1)

    # Ecological model for true abundance (process model)
    for(k in 1:nspec){
    for(i in 1:nsite){
        a[i,k] ~ dbern(phi[k])       # Adjustment for zero-inflation
    for(j in 1:nyear){
        N[j,i,k] ~ dpois(a[i,k]*lambda[j,i,k])
        log(lambda[j,i,k]) <- beta0[k] + beta[k,1]*Locale_Size[j,i,1] + beta[k,2]*Treatment[j,i,1] +
            beta[k,3]*Forb_Cover[j,i,1] + beta[k,4]*X_Coordinate[j,i,1] +
            beta[k,5]*Landscape_Complexity[j,i,1] #+ W[i]

        # Compute presence/absence matrix z (for N > 0) from latent abundance
        z[j,i,k] <- step(N[j,i,k]-1) # Returns TRUE if N >= 0
    }
    }
    }

    #Conditional autoregressive process (e.g., spatial random effects)
    # tau.w ~ dgamma(0.0001, 0.0001)
    # for(i in 1:L){
    #     weights[i] <- 1
    #     W[1:nsite] ~ dcar_normal(adj[1:L], weights[1:L], num[1:nsite], tau.w, zero_mean=1)
    # }

    # Observation model for replicated counts
    for(k in 1:nspec){
    for(j in 1:nyear){
    for(i in 1:nsite){
    for(h in 1:nrep[j]){
        Yc[j,i,h,k] ~ dbin(p[j,i,h,k], N[j,i,k])
        p[j,i,h,k] ~ T(dbeta(tau*mu[j,i,h,k], tau*(1-mu[j,i,h,k])), 0.001, 0.999)
        logit(mu[j,i,h,k]) <- alpha0[k] + alpha[k,1]*Julian_Day[j,i,h] + alpha[k,2]*pow(Julian_Day[j,i,h], 2)
    }
    }
    }
    }

    # Other derived quantities
    for(k in 1:nspec){
        mlambda[k] <- phi[k]*beta0[k]            # Expected abundance on natural scale
    for(j in 1:nyear){
        Nocc.fs[j,k] <- sum(z[j,1:nsite,k])      # Number of occupied sites among survey locations
    }
    }

    for(i in 1:nsite){
    for(j in 1:nyear){
        Nsite[i,j] <- sum(z[j,i,1:nspec])        # Number of occurring species at each survey location
    }
    }
})

nspec <- dim(Ycd)[4] #35
nsite <- dim(Ycd)[2] #14
npred <- 5 #Ecological (abundance) process
ndet <- 2 #Observation (detection) process

const <- list(nyear=dim(Ycd)[1], nsite=dim(Ycd)[2], nrep=c(5,6), nspec=dim(Ycd)[4],
              L=length(winnb$weights), npred=5, ndet=2) #L for when including spatial random effects based on nearest neighbors

# Initial values
ast <- matrix(rep(1, nspec*nsite), nrow=nsite)
some.more <- 5
Nst <- apply(Ycd, c(1,2,4), function(x){max(x, na.rm=T)}) + some.more
Nst[Nst == '-Inf'] <- 5

init <- function() list(a=ast, N=Nst, alpha0=runif(nspec, 0, 0.1), beta0=rnorm(nspec),
                        alpha=matrix(runif(n=nspec*ndet, 0, 0.1), ncol=ndet),
                        beta=matrix(rnorm(n=nspec*npred), ncol=npred),
                        phi=runif(nsite, 0, 1), tau=1, tau.alpha0=1,
                        tau.alpha=1, tau.beta0=1, tau.beta=1) #, tau.w=1, W=rep(1, nsite))

params <- c("phi", "a", "N", "z", "p", "mlambda", "alpha0", "beta0", "alpha", "beta", "mu.beta0", "sd.beta0",
            "mu.beta", "sd.beta", "mu.alpha0L", "mu.alpha0", "sd.alpha0", "mu.alpha", "sd.alpha", "Nsite")

ni <- 1100 ; nt <- 10 ; nb <- 100 ; nc <- 1 #Starting with a shorter MCMC

Rmodel_100 <- nimbleModel(code=code100, constants=const, data=win.data)
outFull_100 <- nimbleMCMC(model=Rmodel_100, inits=init, niter=ni, nchains=nc, nburnin=nb, thin=nt,
                          monitors=params, samples=TRUE, summary=TRUE, WAIC=TRUE,
                          setSeed=TRUE)

Additional information about the input data:
nyear = 2      #Number of survey years
nspec = 35     #Number of recorded species
nsite = 14     #Number of survey locations
nrep = c(5, 6) #Number of replicate surveys per location, 5 during one year and 6 during the other
npred = 5      #Number of predictors on (abundance) process model
ndet = 2       #Number of predictors on (detection) observation model
#nrep: replicate survey 6 in the first year contains NAs for every location
#npred and ndet: all predictors are standardized (i.e. z-scored)
#input data: besides replicate 6 in year 1, there are not other NAs recorded

Based on what I have read in the NIMBLE user manual, as well as in a few posts to the users' group, the errors that I am getting are related to model initialization and/or computing WAIC. Unfortunately, I am also having a difficult time trying to solve the problems.

Any suggestions toward improvement or solution would be much appreciated. Thank you for your help in advance.

Sincerely,
Andrew

messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrew,

Thanks for the question.  The messages may well be separate.  My first guess for the messages about mismatched sizes is that the inits or data objects you are providing do not match the sizes from the model declarations.  For the first one, it is being given something of length 14 that it thinks should be length 35.  When I study your code, it appears that phi is declared to be length 35 (nspec) in the model code but the inits is created as length 14 (nsite).  If I have followed correctly, that could explain the first error message.  If that's correct, maybe you can track down other size mismatches.  If not, please let us know.

The JAGS examples from AHM have been translated to nimble here: https://github.com/nimble-training/AHMnimble  Unfortunately I see that 11.10 was not completed.  I think that means we ran out of time when putting that together and had to move on.  Still I hope the other case might be helpful (and let us know if you want to contribute 11.10!)  (Also the compareMCMCs code in those examples is stale, but the basic code should work.)

-Perry

Hi Andrew,

I don't think so.  The warning about a[1, 1] probably means something is not initialized ok.  Sometimes one could have for example phi[1] == 0, so that the log probability that a[1, 1] == 1 (which looks like its value in inits) is -Inf. Sometimes the MCMC can overcome a -Inf initial value, but sometimes it never moves to valid values.   But your inits for phi don't look like they would have 0.   I don't have your data so I can't reproduce what's going on.

Please try the following

set.seed(1)
Rmodel_100 <- nimbleModel(code=code100, constants=const, data=win.data, inits = init())
Rmodel_100$a[1, 1]
Rmodel_100$phi[1]
Rmodel_100$calculate("a[1, 1]")

Perry

Hi all! Wanted to update on this and get some suggestions.

I ended up resizing my VM to 480gb, and compilation didn't crash this time. However, I wasn't able to monitor how much memory was actually being used once I resized it, so I can't comment on that.

I did this on a third of the data (design matrix: ~10k rows, 31 columns). It took about an hour for buildMCMC to complete, 2 hours for compilation (of project and MCMC together) to complete, and 14.5 hours for the simulation to run 1000 iterations on the compiled object. Ideally, I'd like to run 10k iterations on this, for better mixing. But this doesn't seem scalable if I want to run a longer simulation, include the full dataset, or both. Do you have any thoughts on what could be going on here with the extreme memory usage and the amount of time it takes to complete the simulation?

Thank you!
Liz

However, compilation does not complete and instead crashes R.

messages.body_plain:
That's very helpful.  I'd suggest tracking down some of the NAs from initial values as follows.  Take beta0[1].  I'd look at its parameters, mu.beta0 and tau.beta0.  I don't see those in your inits (but may be looking too hastily), so that could explain the initial NA for the log probability of beta0[1].  When running the MCMC, non-initialized parameters should be drawn from their priors, but sometimes values can be very bad or even incompatible with other parts of the model.  In general a good strategy is to initialize everything.  If you want to track down where the problem is after MCMC initialization, one thing you can do is run the MCMC for 0 iterations -- to trigger the MCMC's initialization but not do any sampling -- and then inspect the state of the model (similar to what you provided -- check values and try calculations).  You can do this with the uncompiled model&mcmc or you can compile both and then do it.  But you'll have to go into a more resolved workflow than nimbleMCMC (see User Manual), which wraps the steps of interest.

Also note that the following motif common from JAGS and WinBUGS is unnecessary in NIMBLE:

tau.beta0 <- pow(sd.beta0, -2)
sd.beta0 ~ dunif(0, 10)

beta0[k] ~ dnorm(mu.beta0, tau=tau.beta0)

In NIMBLE, it's simpler and easier to do:
sd.beta0 ~ dunif(0, 10)
beta0[k] ~ dnorm(mu.beta0, sd=sd.beta0)

Perry

P.S. Unfortunately NIMBLE team response times may decrease over the next few weeks.

messages.body_plain:
Very helpful tips again, Perry. Thanks very much. With Ben Padilla's help off-forum, we did notice that I hadn't yet initialized all of the hyperparameters involved. I will be adding those items next.

Thanks also for the note moving my JAGS/WinBUGS habitual variance syntax to NIMBLE's syntax. I will also make those changes, in order to help simplify the model even further.

In the end, most of what I am experiencing is probably due to habits leftover from using JAGS, and so I will make additional adjustments to NIMBLE's requirements.

Cheers,
Andrew

On Tuesday, August 4, 2020 at 5:11:37 PM UTC-4, pdevalpine wrote:

> That's very helpful.  I'd suggest tracking down some of the NAs from initial values as follows.  Take beta0[1].  I'd look at its parameters, mu.beta0 and tau.beta0.  I don't see those in your inits (but may be looking too hastily), so that could explain the initial NA for the log probability of beta0[1].  When running the MCMC, non-initialized parameters should be drawn from their priors, but sometimes values can be very bad or even incompatible with other parts of the model.  In general a good strategy is to initialize everything.  If you want to track down where the problem is after MCMC initialization, one thing you can do is run the MCMC for 0 iterations -- to trigger the MCMC's initialization but not do any sampling -- and then inspect the state of the model (similar to what you provided -- check values and try calculations).  You can do this with the uncompiled model&mcmc or you can compile both and then do it.  But you'll have to go into a more resolved workflow than nimbleMCMC (see User Manual), which wraps the steps of interest.
>
> Also note that the following motif common from JAGS and WinBUGS is unnecessary in NIMBLE:
>
> tau.beta0 <- pow(sd.beta0, -2)
> sd.beta0 ~ dunif(0, 10)
> beta0[k] ~ dnorm(mu.beta0, tau=tau.beta0)
>
> In NIMBLE, it's simpler and easier to do:
> sd.beta0 ~ dunif(0, 10)
> beta0[k] ~ dnorm(mu.beta0, sd=sd.beta0)
>
> Perry
>
> P.S. Unfortunately NIMBLE team response times may decrease over the next few weeks.

messages.subject: Re: compilation crashes R with large dataset
messages.subject_clean: compilation crashes R with large dataset
messages.body_plain:
Hi Liz,

Perry and I chatted a bit about this case, and I'm following up here. In your model, you specify your spatio-temporal variation using distributions placed on the time series innovations (the phi_sp). This leads to an explosion in the dependencies for the latent process values when the MCMC is being set up and being sampled, which leads to large memory usage and slow sampling. A simple example of this is discussed in materials from our June workshop - see https://github.com/nimble-training/nimble-virtual-2020 in the content/4_improving_mcmc  module under "Think like a graph: reducing dependencies".

Unfortunately the solution posed in that material, which is to 'center' the process at time t on the process at time t-1, won't work with a CAR model because we haven't set up the CAR model to take a vector mean.
An alternative to a CAR structure would be to use a Gaussian process or a spline, which do allow for such centering. We have some details on Gaussian processes and splines, again in our June workshop, in content/7_spatial_models.  The basic idea would be to have something like this as your time-evolving process (I'm omitting the scaling you have with eta and sigma_phi as I just want to illustrate the basic idea):

phi_full[1:s, m, i] ~ dmvnorm(phi_full[1:s, m-1, i], cov = C[1:s, 1:s])

where you'd have to set up "C" as a spatial covariance matrix. Alternatively, you could set up splines to capture the spatial variation and have the spline coefficients evolve over time.

In general, getting good MCMC performance for a large spatio-temporal problem like this can be hard. This will particularly be the case if the number of spatial locations, 's', gets into the thousands.

-chris

messages.subject: User-defined dirichlet-multinomial distribution
messages.subject_clean: User-defined dirichlet-multinomial distribution
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

In the User Manual Version 0.9.1, Section 12.2 describes user-defined distributions. An example is given for a multivariate Dirichlet-multinomial distribution which defines the log probability:

    logProb <- lgamma(size) - sum(lgamma(x)) + lgamma(sum(alpha)) -
      sum(lgamma(alpha)) + sum(lgamma(alpha + x)) - lgamma(sum(alpha) + size)

Should it instead be this?:

    logProb <- lgamma(size+1) - sum(lgamma(x+1)) + lgamma(sum(alpha)) -
      sum(lgamma(alpha)) + sum(lgamma(alpha + x)) - lgamma(sum(alpha) + size)

This would follow from the Dirichlet-multinomial pdf, which has factorial(size) in the numerator and prod(factorial(x)) in the denominator, with factorial(x)=gamma(x+1). Please let me know if I'm making a simple mistake!

Of course, the terms in question don't depend on alpha, so this shouldn't make a difference for MCMC purposes, but I wanted to check since those terms are included in the manual.

Thanks for your time,
Michael

messages.body_plain:
Nice catch, Michael.  Thanks for your detailed reading of the User Manual, and pointing out this error.  Your calculations are correct, and we've just updated the User Manual to include the correct log-probability calculation taking place in the custom distribution ddirchmulti, as appearing in Section 12.2 of the User Manual.  This change will be included in our next upcoming release, which should take place in the next weeks / month or so.

Cheers,
Daniel

On Wednesday, August 5, 2020 at 8:34:15 AM UTC-6 christophe...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Liz,
>
> Perry and I chatted a bit about this case, and I'm following up here. In your model, you specify your spatio-temporal variation using distributions placed on the time series innovations (the phi_sp). This leads to an explosion in the dependencies for the latent process values when the MCMC is being set up and being sampled, which leads to large memory usage and slow sampling. A simple example of this is discussed in materials from our June workshop - see https://github.com/nimble-training/nimble-virtual-2020 in the content/4_improving_mcmc  module under "Think like a graph: reducing dependencies".
>
> Unfortunately the solution posed in that material, which is to 'center' the process at time t on the process at time t-1, won't work with a CAR model because we haven't set up the CAR model to take a vector mean.
> An alternative to a CAR structure would be to use a Gaussian process or a spline, which do allow for such centering. We have some details on Gaussian processes and splines, again in our June workshop, in content/7_spatial_models.  The basic idea would be to have something like this as your time-evolving process (I'm omitting the scaling you have with eta and sigma_phi as I just want to illustrate the basic idea):
>
> phi_full[1:s, m, i] ~ dmvnorm(phi_full[1:s, m-1, i], cov = C[1:s, 1:s])
>
> where you'd have to set up "C" as a spatial covariance matrix. Alternatively, you could set up splines to capture the spatial variation and have the spline coefficients evolve over time.
>
> In general, getting good MCMC performance for a large spatio-temporal problem like this can be hard. This will particularly be the case if the number of spatial locations, 's', gets into the thousands.
>
> -chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I found another solution and thought I'd post it here so it's documented. nimble can be included as a suggested package in another package (i.e., under Suggests in the description) by using the commands:

requireNamespace(nimble)
attachNamespace("nimble")

The first line is the recommended mechanisms for loading suggested packages. The second which I've added attaches the namespace so that functions in the package can be seen globally. This avoids direct use of library(nimble) within the package which generates a note when the package is checked.

I have a feeling that this may be counter to the spirit of not using library() (I think I've essentially recreated what library() does), but it works and does not raise any issues during the checks.

Thanks all for your help,

Simon

messages.subject_clean: spatial mark resight activity center sampler for unmarked individuals
messages.body_plain:
Following up on this many months later. I'm can't figure out how to do 2 things for a spatial capture-recapture type sampler. Both concern the activity center update, which I'm replacing with a custom update.

1. I want to get the dependencies for 1 activity center at a time, but c++ doesn't understand the "paste" command (in red below). This does work in R, which does know "paste".  Is there a way to extract the dependencies for one activity center at a time when specifying a single update for all activity centers (target is s[1;M,1;2])?

2. I'm unsure if I am successfully making this sampler adapt. I want it to adapt a single scale parameter for all activity centers, which is only used when each z[i]==1. I attempt to tell it to adapt when replacing the sampler (below in blue), but getScaleHistory() does not return anything, while it does for RW samplers that are not custom (following nimble manual section 7.5.2). Also, I'm unsure how nimble counts acceptances. Will it count them for z[i]==0 updates? I don't want that to happen.

Any help would be much appreciated!

Ben

myActivityCenterSampler <- nimbleFunction(
  contains = sampler_BASE,
  setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control) {
    # Defined stuff

    scale<-1
    xlim<-control$xlim
    ylim<-control$ylim
    M<-control$M

  },

  run = function() {
    # grab current value of z

    z <- model$z
    for(i in 1:M){
      browser()
      calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(paste("s[",i,",1:2]"))
      ## If z==0 propose activity center and accept with probability 1.0
      if(z[i]==0){

        # store proposal into model

        model$s[i, 1:2] <<- c(runif(1, xlim[1], xlim[2]), runif(1, ylim[1], ylim[2]))

        # update dependencies
        model$calculate(calcNodes)

        # Accept candidate trajectory with probability 1.0 and keep the model and mvSaved objects consistent

        copy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)

      }else{#z.curr[i]==1

        # initial model logProb
        model_lp_initial <- model$getLogProb(calcNodes)

        #truncated normal proposal
        sx <- qnorm(runif(1, pnorm(xlim[1], model$s[i, 1], sd=scale), pnorm(xlim[2], model$s[i, 1], sd=scale)), model$s[i, 1], sd=scale)
        sy <- qnorm(runif(1, pnorm(ylim[1], model$s[i, 2], sd=scale), pnorm(ylim[2], model$s[i, 2], sd=scale)), model$s[i, 2], sd=scale)
        model$s[i, 1:2] <<- c(sx, sy)

        # proposal model logProb
        model_lp_proposed <- model$calculate(calcNodes)

        # log-Metropolis-Hastings ratio
        log_MH_ratio <- model_lp_proposed - model_lp_initial
        # Metropolis-Hastings step: determine whether or
        # not to accept the newly proposed value

        jump <- decide(log_MH_ratio)
        if(jump) {

          copy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)
        } else {
          copy(from = mvSaved, to = model, row = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)
        }

      }#z==1
    }
  },
  methods = list( reset = function () {} )
)

conf$removeSampler("s")
conf$addSampler(target = paste(paste("s[1:",M,",1:2]"),sep=""),
                    type = 'myActivityCenterSampler',control = list(xlim=xlims,ylim=ylims,M=M,
                            adaptive=TRUE, adaptInterval=100), #there has to be a better way to assign this stuff
                    silent = TRUE)

> Hi Ben,
>
> Sorry this fell by the wayside for a while.
>
> I can offer several suggestions.
>
> One way to simplify this for other users would be to write a function that manages the sampler assignments.  That eases the burden of learning nimble if you want to share what you develop with others.
>
> For the samplers themselves, here are a few ideas.
>
> It's possible to write one "sampler" (i.e. item on the sampler list) that contains many actual samplers (i.e. nimbleFunctions that do an MCMC update).  The many samplers can then share tuning parameter(s).  This would allow them to tune to average acceptance rate across all activity centers, not each separately.
>
> I didn't follow what you meant by "a single, non-adaptive random walk sampler for z[i]=1 individuals."  Each sampler object targets one node (or nodes).  Maybe you meant what I just tried to describe?
>
> On your idea of having sampler behavior depend on system state(s): In general, one must be careful about this, but I think your specific suggestion would be valid.  If the proposal scale for updating z is made to depend on the value of z, the sampler will not be valid unless care is taken to make the ratio of backward/forward proposal densities in the acceptance probability correct.  But you are suggesting that the proposal scale for updating one value depends on a different parameter that would not change.  That should be valid.
>
> -Perry

messages.body_plain:
Ben, this is extremely hasty because I'm off in just 15 minutes, but here's the gist.

1. The modified code below shows (at least how I would) do what you're trying to do.  Short answer, you can't use "paste" in compiled execution, all node names, and sets of nodes, must be predefined in setup code.  Here we use a nimbleFunctionList.  See the modifications throughout.  Caution.  I have not run, or executed this code, so be very wary of typos, or minor errors, there certainly are some.

2. This is no "bigger system for sampler adaptation".  It's sampler-by-sampler. Everything the RW sampler does to adapt is in the RW sampler code, see on GitHub.  Just supplying adaptive=TRUE, and adaptItnerval in the control list won't do anything.  To adapt the scale parameter, you'll need to include custom code (in the sampler) to do that.  You might follow the code in RW sampler as a model, or in your case, record the total number of successful (and failed) transitions, and use that.  I'd look at the sampler_RW code, and everything in there having to do with adaptation, and go from there.

Good luck.  Modified code below.

myActivityCenterSampler_helperBASE <- nimbleFunctionVirtual(
    name = 'myActivityCenterSampler_helperBASE',
    methods = list(
        calc = function() { returnType(double()) },
        setValue = function(newValue = double(1)) { },
        copyToMVsaved = function() { },
        copyToModel = function() { },
        getLP = function() { returnType(double()) }
    )
)

myActivityCenterSampler_helper <- nimbleFunction(
    name = 'myActivityCenterSampler_helper',
    contains = myActivityCenterSampler_helperBASE,
    setup = function(model, node, mvSaved) {
        calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(node)
    },
    run = function() { print('should never run') },
    methods = list(
        calc = function() {
            returnType(double(0))
            lp <- model$calculate(calcNodes)
            return(lp)
        },
        setValue = function(newValue = double(1)) {
            values(model, node) <<- newValue
        },
        copyToMVsaved = function() {

            copy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)

        },
        copyToModel = function() {

            copy(from = mvSaved, to = model, row = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)

        },
        getLP = function() {
            returnType(double())
            lp <- model$getLogProb(calcNodes)
            return(lp)
        }
    )
)

myActivityCenterSampler <- nimbleFunction(
    contains = sampler_BASE,
    setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control) {
        # Defined stuff
        scale<-1
        xlim<-control$xlim
        ylim<-control$ylim
        M<-control$M

        nfList <- nimbleFunctionList(myActivityCenterSampler_helperBASE)
        for(i in 1:M) {
            node <- paste("s[",i,",1:2]")
            nfList[[i]] <- myActivityCenterSampler_helper(model, node, mvSaved)

        }

    },

    run = function() {
        # grab current value of z
        z <- model$z
        for(i in 1:M){
            browser()

            ##calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(paste("s[",i,",1:2]"))

            ## If z==0 propose activity center and accept with probability 1.0
            if(z[i]==0){

                # store proposal into model

                ##model$s[i, 1:2] <<- c(runif(1, xlim[1], xlim[2]), runif(1, ylim[1], ylim[2]))
                nfList[[i]]$setValue(c(runif(1, xlim[1], xlim[2]), runif(1, ylim[1], ylim[2])))

                # update dependencies
                ##model$calculate(calcNodes)
                nfList[[i]]$calc()

                # Accept candidate trajectory with probability 1.0 and keep the model and mvSaved objects consistent

                ##copy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)
                nfList[[i]]$copyToMVsaved()

            }else{#z.curr[i]==1

                # initial model logProb

                ##model_lp_initial <- model$getLogProb(calcNodes)
                model_lp_initial <- nfList[[i]]$getLP

                #truncated normal proposal
                sx <- qnorm(runif(1, pnorm(xlim[1], model$s[i, 1], sd=scale), pnorm(xlim[2], model$s[i, 1], sd=scale)), model$s[i, 1], sd=scale)
                sy <- qnorm(runif(1, pnorm(ylim[1], model$s[i, 2], sd=scale), pnorm(ylim[2], model$s[i, 2], sd=scale)), model$s[i, 2], sd=scale)

                ##model$s[i, 1:2] <<- c(sx, sy)
                nfList[[i]]$setValue(c(sx, sy))

                # proposal model logProb
                ##model_lp_proposed <- model$calculate(calcNodes)
                model_lp_proposed <- nfList[[i]]$calc()

                # log-Metropolis-Hastings ratio
                log_MH_ratio <- model_lp_proposed - model_lp_initial
                # Metropolis-Hastings step: determine whether or
                # not to accept the newly proposed value
                jump <- decide(log_MH_ratio)
                if(jump) {

                    ##copy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

I apologize if the code below doesn't format in the post correctly, but I can't seem to relocate the forum's button for properly inserting code.

Inspired by additional help off list, I re-coded my community N-mixture model as well as the dimensions of its inputs, and I also added new species-specific (random-intercept) effects to the model for each year.

Here's my latest program:
{
code100 <- nimbleCode({

  # Community priors (with hyperparameters) for species-specific parameters
  for(k in 1:nspec){

    phi[k] ~ dunif(0, 1)                                                                                # adjustment for zero-inflation, and there is plenty of it due to several (sparse) species

    # Alpha parameters (detection)
    for(s in 1:nyear){
      alpha0[k,s] ~ dnorm(mu.alpha0[s], sd=sd.alpha0[s])                   # year-specific intercept on detection
    }
    alpha1[k] ~ dnorm(mu.alpha1, sd=sd.alpha1)                                # linear julian day on detection (z-scored)
    alpha2[k] ~ dnorm(mu.alpha2, sd=sd.alpha2)                                # quadratic julian day on detection (z-scored)

    # Beta parameters (abundance)
    for(s in 1:nyear){
      beta0[k,s] ~ dnorm(mu.beta0[s], sd=sd.beta0[s])                        # year-specific intercept on abundance
    }
    beta1[k] ~ dnorm(mu.beta1, sd=sd.beta1)                                     # locale size on abundance (z-scored)
    beta2[k] ~ dnorm(mu.beta2, sd=sd.beta2)                                     # treatment type (dummy coded) on abundance (categorical indicator)
    beta3[k] ~ dnorm(mu.beta3, sd=sd.beta3)                                     # forb (mean) cover on abundance (z-scored)
    beta4[k] ~ dnorm(mu.beta4, sd=sd.beta4)                                     # longitude on abundance (temporary proxy for spatial autocorrelation; z-scored)
    beta5[k] ~ dnorm(mu.beta5, sd=sd.beta5)                                     # landscape complexity scores on abundance (z-scored)

  }

  # Hyperpriors for community hyperparameters
  # abundance model

  for(s in 1:nyear){
      mu.beta0[s] ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
      sd.beta0[s] ~ dunif(0, 10)
  }
  mu.beta1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
  sd.beta1 ~ dunif(0, 10)
  mu.beta2 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
  sd.beta2 ~ dunif(0, 10)
  mu.beta3 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
  sd.beta3 ~ dunif(0, 10)
  mu.beta4 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
  sd.beta4 ~ dunif(0, 10)
  mu.beta5 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
  sd.beta5 ~ dunif(0, 10)

  # detection model
  for(s in 1:nyear){
    mu.alpha0[s] ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
    sd.alpha0[s] ~ dunif(0, 10)
  }
  mu.alpha1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
  sd.alpha1 ~ dunif(0, 10)
  mu.alpha2 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
  sd.alpha2 ~ dunif(0, 10)

  #Conditional autoregressive process (e.g., spatial random fields)
  # tau.w ~ dgamma(0.001, 0.001)
  # for(i in 1:L){
  #     weights[i] <- 1
  #     W[1:nsite] ~ dcar_normal(adj[1:L], weights[1:L], num[1:nsite], tau.w, zero_mean=1)
  # }

  # Ecological model for true abundance (process model)
  for(k in 1:nspec){
    for(i in 1:nsite){
      a[i,k] ~ dbern(phi[k])

      N[i,k] ~ dpois(a[i,k] * lambda[i,k])
      log(lambda[i,k]) <- beta0[k, year[i]] + beta1[k] * LocaleSize[i] + beta2[k] * Treatment[i] + beta3[k] * ForbCover[i] +
                          beta4[k] * Longitude[i] + beta5[k] * LandscapeComplexity[i] #+ W[i]

      # Compute presence/absence matrix z (for N > 0) from latent abundance

      z[i,k] <- step(N[i,k]-1)  # returns TRUE if N >= 0
    }
  }

  #Simple (naive) detection specification
  #alphaP ~ dunif(0, 10)
  #betaP ~ dunif(0, 10)

  #Beta-binomial (informed) detection specification
  #tau <- exp(tau.log)
  #tau.log ~ dnorm(0, 1)

  # Observation model for replicated counts
  for(k in 1:nspec){

    for(i in 1:nsite){
      for(j in 1:nrep[year[i]]){
        Yc[i,j,k] ~ dbin(p[i,j,k], N[i,k])
        logit(p[i,j,k]) <- alpha0[k, year[i]] + alpha1[k] * JulianDay[i] + alpha2[k] * pow(JulianDay[i], 2)

        #Beta-binomial (naive or informed) specification
        #p[i,j, k] ~ T(dbeta(alphaP, betaP), 0.001, 0.999)                                  #Naive specification
        #p[i,j,k] ~ T(dbeta(tau*mu[i,j,k], tau*(1-mu[i,j,k])), 0.001, 0.999)         #Informed specification
        #logit(mu[i,j,k]) <- (insert model above)                                                 #Informed specification

      }
    }
  }

  # Other derived quantities
  for(k in 1:nspec){

    for(s in 1:nyear){
      mlambda[k,s] <- phi[k] * exp(beta0[k,s])                               # Expected abundance on natural scale
      logit(mp[k,s]) <- alpha0[k,s]                                                    # Mean detection on natural scale
    }
    Nocc.fs[k] <- sum(z[1:nsite,k])                                                 # Number of occupied sites of the total
  }
  for (i in 1:nsite) {
    Nrich[i] <- sum(z[i,1:nspec])                                                     # Number of occurring species at each site
    Nbirds[i] <- sum(N[i,1:nspec])                                                  # Number of total individuals at each site
  }
})

nyear <- 2
nsite <- dim(Ycd)[1]
nrep <- c(dim(Ycd)[2]-1, dim(Ycd)[2]) #5 replicate visits made to sites in year 1; whereas, 6 were made to sites in year 2
nspec <- dim(Ycd)[3]

const <- list(year=c(rep(1,14),rep(2,14)), nyear=nyear, nsite=nsite, nrep=nrep, nspec=nspec,
              L=length(winnb$weights)) #Currently, not using L just yet (e.g., for future CAR process to help account for spatial autocorrelation)

# prepare initial values
ast <- matrix(rep(1, dim(Ycd)[3] * dim(Ycd)[1]),
              nrow = dim(Ycd)[1])                                                          # All species will begin as present
some.more <- 5
Nst <- apply(Ycd, c(1,3), max, na.rm = T) + some.more           # initial abundance > obs abundance
init <- function() list( # starting values for latent N and its dependents
                         a = ast,
                         phi = runif(dim(Ycd)[3],0,1),
                         N = Nst,                                                                   # starting values for the species specific abundance

                         # starting values for community parameters
                         alpha0 = matrix(rnorm(dim(Ycd)[3]*nyear),
                                         nrow = dim(Ycd)[3], ncol = nyear),     # starting value for detection intercept (species-specific)
                         beta0 = matrix(rnorm(dim(Ycd)[3]*nyear),
                                        nrow = dim(Ycd)[3], ncol = nyear),      # starting value for abundance intercept (species-specific)
                         alpha1 = rnorm(dim(Ycd)[3]),                             # linear julian day on detection
                         beta1 = rnorm(dim(Ycd)[3]),                               # locale size on abundance
                         alpha2 = rnorm(dim(Ycd)[3]),                             # quadratic julian day on detection
                         beta2 = rnorm(dim(Ycd)[3]),                               # treatment type (dummy coded) on abundance
                         beta3 = rnorm(dim(Ycd)[3]),                               # forb (mean) cover on abundance
                         beta4 = rnorm(dim(Ycd)[3]),                               # longitude on abundance
                         beta5 = rnorm(dim(Ycd)[3]),                               # landscape complexity scores on abundance

                         # starting values for community hyperparameters
                         mu.alpha0 = rnorm(2),
                         mu.beta0 = rnorm(2),
                         sd.beta0 = runif(2,0,5),
                         sd.alpha0 = runif(2,0,5),
                         mu.alpha1 = rnorm(1),
                         sd.alpha1 = runif(1,0,5),
                         mu.alpha2 = rnorm(1),
                         sd.alpha2 = runif(1,0,5),
                         mu.beta1 = rnorm(1),
                         sd.beta1 = runif(1,0,5),
                         mu.beta2 = rnorm(1),
                         sd.beta2 = runif(1,0,5),
                         mu.beta3 = rnorm(1),
                         sd.beta3 = runif(1,0,5),
                         mu.beta4 = rnorm(1),
                         sd.beta4 = runif(1,0,5),
                         mu.beta5 = rnorm(1),
                         sd.beta5 = runif(1,0,5))

params <- c("phi", "a", "N", "z", "p", "mlambda", "mp",
            "beta0", "mu.beta0", "sd.beta0",
            "beta1", "mu.beta1", "sd.beta1", "beta2", "mu.beta2", "sd.beta2", "beta3", "mu.beta3", "sd.beta3",
            "beta4", "mu.beta4", "sd.beta4", "beta5", "mu.beta5", "sd.beta5",
            "alpha0", "mu.alpha0", "sd.alpha0",
            "alpha1", "mu.alpha1", "sd.alpha1", "alpha2", "mu.alpha2", "sd.alpha2",
            "Nrich", "Nbirds")

ni <- 1100 ; nt <- 10 ; nb <- 100 ; nc <- 3  #Shortened for a test run

Rmodel_100 <- nimbleModel(code=code100, constants=const, data=win.data, inits = init())

outFull_100 <- nimbleMCMC(model=Rmodel_100, niter=ni, nchains=nc, nburnin=nb, thin=nt,

                          monitors=params, samples=TRUE, summary=TRUE, WAIC=TRUE,
                          setSeed=TRUE)
}

Soon after running the MCMC (i.e. using default configurations), I receive multiples of the following warning message at different indices for latent N:
{
"Warning: slice sampler reached maximum number of contractions for 'N[14, 35]'. Current parameter value is 5."
}

Throughout the many warnings, "5" varies (sometimes >5) from time to time, and when a "5" is listed, I suspect that this is due to 0 (count) records for particular cells (i.e. indexed by site i, replicate visit j, and species k), which is later defined by my specified initial values for latent N (see Nst and some.more in the code above). Searching the user manual and forum has only turned up a few, seemingly unrelated, examples.

Does anyone have any recommendations as to what I could do to help resolve this issue? Should I simply change the default (slice) sampler for N to something else entirely? Could there be something else wrong? For instance, due to several survey limitations, some input variables are numerically similar at sites between years (e.g., LocaleSize and JulianDay change between years, but Treatment, ForbCover, Longitude, and LandscapeComplexity do not).

Finally, do any initialization conditions of the model appear problematic? Recall that I am using z-scored predictors in the abundance (process) and detection (observation) submodels.

I sincerely appreciate your continued assistance in advance.

Best,
Andrew

> Ben, this is extremely hasty because I'm off in just 15 minutes, but here's the gist.
>
> 1. The modified code below shows (at least how I would) do what you're trying to do.  Short answer, you can't use "paste" in compiled execution, all node names, and sets of nodes, must be predefined in setup code.  Here we use a nimbleFunctionList.  See the modifications throughout.  Caution.  I have not run, or executed this code, so be very wary of typos, or minor errors, there certainly are some.
>
> 2. This is no "bigger system for sampler adaptation".  It's sampler-by-sampler. Everything the RW sampler does to adapt is in the RW sampler code, see on GitHub.  Just supplying adaptive=TRUE, and adaptItnerval in the control list won't do anything.  To adapt the scale parameter, you'll need to include custom code (in the sampler) to do that.  You might follow the code in RW sampler as a model, or in your case, record the total number of successful (and failed) transitions, and use that.  I'd look at the sampler_RW code, and everything in there having to do with adaptation, and go from there.
>
> Good luck.  Modified code below.

I attempt to tell it to adapt when replacing the sampler (below in blue), but getScaleHistory() does not return anything, while it does for RW samplers that are not custom (following nimble manual section 7.5.2). Also, I'm unsure how nimble counts acceptances. Will it count them for z[i]==0 updates? I don't want that to happen.

> > > Hi Ben,
> > >
> > > Sorry this fell by the wayside for a while.
> > >
> > > I can offer several suggestions.
> > >
> > > One way to simplify this for other users would be to write a function that manages the sampler assignments.  That eases the burden of learning nimble if you want to share what you develop with others.
> > >
> > > For the samplers themselves, here are a few ideas.
> > >
> > > It's possible to write one "sampler" (i.e. item on the sampler list) that contains many actual samplers (i.e. nimbleFunctions that do an MCMC update).  The many samplers can then share tuning parameter(s).  This would allow them to tune to average acceptance rate across all activity centers, not each separately.
> > >
> > > I didn't follow what you meant by "a single, non-adaptive random walk sampler for z[i]=1 individuals."  Each sampler object targets one node (or nodes).  Maybe you meant what I just tried to describe?
> > >
> > > On your idea of having sampler behavior depend on system state(s): In general, one must be careful about this, but I think your specific suggestion would be valid.  If the proposal scale for updating z is made to depend on the value of z, the sampler will not be valid unless care is taken to make the ratio of backward/forward proposal densities in the acceptance probability correct.  But you are suggesting that the proposal scale for updating one value depends on a different parameter that would not change.  That should be valid.
> > >
> > > -Perry

> > > >
> > > > This solution for NIMBLE is the same as I use in R, so I don't loose anything switching to NIMBLE here. I'm just wondering if there is a way to leverage NIMBLE functionality so that the user does not need to be an expert on activity center mixing in these models. The only idea I have is perhaps NIMBLE can tune 2 proposal parameters for you in a custom update and you apply one to the situation where z[i]=1 and sum(y[i,]=0) and another to the situation where z[i]=1 and sum(y[i,]>0). z[i]=0 are then proposed from the prior. Absent a major model specification, the unmarked activity center acceptance rates will necessarily be at least decent. But that rule of thumb isn't available for similar models with no marked individuals. In either case, we shouldn't let nimble select or tune it.

messages.body_plain:
With the help of a colleague off list, I was able to identify and correct the "slice sampler" errors for latent N.

In my code, I wrapped my model statement with the following:
{
#Set up a log file
con <- file("test.log")
sink(con, append=TRUE)
sink(con, append=TRUE, type="message")

# This will echo all input and not truncate 150+ character lines...
source(outFull_100 <- nimbleMCMC(model=Rmodel_100, niter=ni, nchains=nc, nburnin=nb, thin=nt,
                                 monitors=params, samples=TRUE, summary=TRUE, WAIC=TRUE,
                                 setSeed=TRUE), echo=TRUE, max.deparse.length=10000)

# Restore output to console
sink()
sink(type="message")
}

Viewing the front end of that new log file (e.g., to work around console print limits in RStudio), revealed a bug in my code for preparing the model's input data (i.e. one process-level predictor contained NAs).

That said, however, I still get the following error after initial MCMC completion (i.e. a shortened run based on ~1000 total iterations for now):
{
"Error in quantile.default(x, 0.025) :   missing values and NaN's not allowed if 'na.rm' is FALSE."
}

Perhaps this could be because of how/where I attempt to skip over empty (NA) records in the count data (e.g., technicians did not conduct a sixth replicate survey in the first year, but they did in the second year).

Referencing my last post, here's the code snippet in which I attempt to skip over missing sixth replicates per site and species in the first year (e.g., nrep=c(5, 6) and year=c(rep(1, nsite), rep(2, nsite)), and so total j=5 when year=1 and total j=6 when year=2):
{

  # Observation model for replicated counts
  for(k in 1:nspec){
    for(i in 1:nsite){
      for(j in 1:nrep[year[i]]){
        Yc[i,j,k] ~ dbin(p[i,j,k], N[i,k])
        logit(p[i,j,k]) <- alpha0[k, year[i]] + alpha1[k] * JulianDay[i] + alpha2[k] * pow(JulianDay[i], 2)
      }
    }
  }

}

Any suggestions on how to fix the quantile error would be much appreciated. Thanks again!

Andrew

I don't see those in your inits (but may be looking too hastily), so that could explain the initial NA for the log probability of beta0[1].  When running the MCMC, non-initialized parameters should be drawn from their priors, but sometimes values can be very bad or even incompatible with other parts of the model.  In general a good strategy is to initialize everything.  If you want to track down where the problem is after MCMC initialization, one thing you can do is run the MCMC for 0 iterations -- to trigger the MCMC's initialization but not do any sampling -- and then inspect the state of the model (similar to what you provided -- check values and try calculations). messages.body_plain:
For those interested in this problem, I was able to solve the {  "Error in quantile.default(x, 0.025) :   missing values and NaN's not allowed if 'na.rm' is FALSE."  } problem with the help of a colleague, as well as Daniel Turek, off list.

I identified that the reason for the quantile( ) error was related to my purposeful (though misinformed) "skipping" over certain NA records in the input count data, particularly in the loop over j replicates for the observation model.

Thinking that (like JAGS) NIMBLE might impute values for those missing counts, and also suggested by the user manual, I removed the { nrep[year[i]] } statement from my loop over j and then replaced it with the total number of possible replicates (e.g., regardless of the missing sixth replicate survey for every site in the first year). This helped the MCMC run to completion without error, and so I will now run the model much longer and evaluate parameter results/convergence.

In other words, I think that I have found a workable solution for the time being. Here's hoping that new (forthcoming) complexities (e.g., beta-binomial detection, p, as well as spatial random effects, W) do not further inhibit the MCMCs.

Thank you all for your kindness and generosity. I sincerely appreciate the helpfulness of the members of this user group!

Onward,
Andrew

Solution to the quantile( ) error,
From:
{

  # Observation model for replicated counts
  for(k in 1:nspec){
    for(i in 1:nsite){

      for(j in 1:nrep[year[i]]){ #Skipping over NA counts of the (missing) sixth replicate survey in year 1

        Yc[i,j,k] ~ dbin(p[i,j,k], N[i,k])
        logit(p[i,j,k]) <- alpha0[k, year[i]] + alpha1[k] * JulianDay[i] + alpha2[k] * pow(JulianDay[i], 2)
      }
    }
  }

}

To:
{

  # Observation model for replicated counts
  for(k in 1:nspec){
    for(i in 1:nsite){

      for(j in 1:max(nrep)){ #Allowing the model to impute counts to the (missing) sixth replicate survey in year 1

        Yc[i,j,k] ~ dbin(p[i,j,k], N[i,k])
        logit(p[i,j,k]) <- alpha0[k, year[i]] + alpha1[k] * JulianDay[i] + alpha2[k] * pow(JulianDay[i], 2)
      }
    }
  }

}

When running the MCMC, non-initialized parameters should be drawn from their priors, but sometimes values can be very bad or even incompatible with other parts of the model. If you want to track down where the problem is after MCMC initialization, one thing you can do is run the MCMC for 0 iterations -- to trigger the MCMC's initialization but not do any sampling -- and then inspect the state of the model (similar to what you provided -- check values and try calculations). messages.subject: Re: compilation crashes R with large dataset
messages.subject_clean: compilation crashes R with large dataset
messages.body_plain:
In case anyone is interested or has a similar issue in the future, I was able to get the below code to work rather quickly! As before, I did this on a third of the data (design matrix: ~10k rows, 31 columns). The max memory used was ~20gb. It took ~30sec for buildMCMC to complete, ~3min for compilation to complete, and ~9.5 hours for the simulation to run 5000 iterations.

The "spatio-temporal effects" chunk in my nimble code now looks like this:
  zeros_phi[1:s] <- rep(0, s)
  for(i in 1:2) {
    # create precision matrix for dmnorm
    prec_mat[1:s, 1:s, i] <- (1/sigma_phi[i])^2 * tau[i] * (iden[1:s, 1:s] - gamma[i] * C[1:s, 1:s]) %*% M_inv[1:s, 1:s]

    # initialize first timestep
    phi[1:s, 1, i] ~ dmnorm(zeros_phi[1:s], prec = prec_mat[1:s, 1:s, i])

    # all subsequent timesteps for each of the s=84 regions
    for(m in 2:t) {
      eta_phi[1:s, m-1, i] <- eta[i] * phi[1:s, m-1, i]
      phi[1:s, m, i] ~ dmnorm(eta_phi[1:s, m-1, i], prec = prec_mat[1:s, 1:s, i])
    }
  }

With the appropriate variables calculated as follows:
CM <- as.carCM(nbInfo$adj, nbInfo$weights, nbInfo$num) (note: nbInfo previously defined for neighborhood data)
C <- sweep(W, 1, rowSums(W), FUN="/") # row-normalized weight matrix (each row sums to 1); W is unnormalized weight matrix for the 84 spatial regions
M_inv <- solve(diag(CM$M)) # diagonal matrix of inverses of conditional variances
gamma_bounds <- carBounds(CM$C, nbInfo$adj, nbInfo$num, CM$M)
gam_min = gamma_bounds[1]; gam_max = gamma_bounds[2]
[note: added prior on gamma in earlier part of code; gamma ~ unif(gam_min, gam_max)]

Thank you again, Chris and Perry, for your help with this!

best,
Liz

On Thursday, August 6, 2020 at 7:58:43 PM UTC-6 Liz Lawler wrote:
> Hi Chris,
>
> Thank you so much for your detailed response! I'm going to take a look at the resources you provided and work on implementing these changes. I'll report back, just in case anyone is curious!
>
> best,
> Liz
>
> On Wednesday, August 5, 2020 at 8:34:15 AM UTC-6 christophe...@gmail.com wrote:
> > Hi Liz,
> >
> > Perry and I chatted a bit about this case, and I'm following up here. In your model, you specify your spatio-temporal variation using distributions placed on the time series innovations (the phi_sp). This leads to an explosion in the dependencies for the latent process values when the MCMC is being set up and being sampled, which leads to large memory usage and slow sampling. A simple example of this is discussed in materials from our June workshop - see https://github.com/nimble-training/nimble-virtual-2020 in the content/4_improving_mcmc  module under "Think like a graph: reducing dependencies".
> >
> > Unfortunately the solution posed in that material, which is to 'center' the process at time t on the process at time t-1, won't work with a CAR model because we haven't set up the CAR model to take a vector mean.
> > An alternative to a CAR structure would be to use a Gaussian process or a spline, which do allow for such centering. We have some details on Gaussian processes and splines, again in our June workshop, in content/7_spatial_models.  The basic idea would be to have something like this as your time-evolving process (I'm omitting the scaling you have with eta and sigma_phi as I just want to illustrate the basic idea):
> >
> > phi_full[1:s, m, i] ~ dmvnorm(phi_full[1:s, m-1, i], cov = C[1:s, 1:s])
> >
> > where you'd have to set up "C" as a spatial covariance matrix. Alternatively, you could set up splines to capture the spatial variation and have the spline coefficients evolve over time.
> >
> > In general, getting good MCMC performance for a large spatio-temporal problem like this can be hard. This will particularly be the case if the number of spatial locations, 's', gets into the thousands.
> >
> > -chris
> >
> > On Tue, Aug 4, 2020 at 11:56 AM Liz Lawler <esla...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Hi all! Wanted to update on this and get some suggestions.
> > >
> > > I ended up resizing my VM to 480gb, and compilation didn't crash this time. However, I wasn't able to monitor how much memory was actually being used once I resized it, so I can't comment on that.
> > >
> > > I did this on a third of the data (design matrix: ~10k rows, 31 columns). It took about an hour for buildMCMC to complete, 2 hours for compilation (of project and MCMC together) to complete, and 14.5 hours for the simulation to run 1000 iterations on the compiled object. Ideally, I'd like to run 10k iterations on this, for better mixing. But this doesn't seem scalable if I want to run a longer simulation, include the full dataset, or both. Do you have any thoughts on what could be going on here with the extreme memory usage and the amount of time it takes to complete the simulation?
> > >
> > > Thank you!
> > > Liz
> > >
> > > On Saturday, August 1, 2020 at 9:26:49 PM UTC-6 Liz Lawler wrote:
> > > > Hello!
> > > >
> > > > First, I want to say thank you for all the help you've provided thus far with nimble - I really appreciate it. Your suggestions have made my model run considerably faster!
> > > >
> > > > Second, I'm currently having an issue with compilation when I expand my model to include more data. The code below works for a small number of timesteps (t = 4; 336 observations, 31 columns) and quickly gets through every phase of building and running the model. I'd like to eventually run the model on around 360 timesteps (~30k observations, 31 columns). As an intermediate step to determine how long it would take to run the full model, I wanted to first test it on a third of the data. Every step through buildMCMC works, and then compilation runs for a bit and crashes. nimbleModel took 5.5 sec, configureMCMC took < 1 sec, and buildMCMC took ~ 55 minutes. However, compilation does not complete and instead crashes R.
> > > >
> > > > I'm doing all of this through google cloud computing, so initially, I ran this on a VM with 64gb memory. When compilation approached ~ 64gb usage of memory, it crashed, so I figured I'd expand the VM to 128gb and try again. R again crashed at ~ 125gb of memory. If this truly is a memory problem, I'm happy to keep expanding the memory, but I'm hoping there's another way to do this! Any suggestions on what to do?
> > > >
> > > > Steps I've taken to speed up the model and get this to work include leaving my design matrix in R and vectorizing beta to reduce the nodes from ~5000 to 168 multivariate elements. For reference, here is what the current configuration with a third of the data looks like:
> > > >
> > > > ===== Monitors =====
> > > > thin = 1: alpha, eta, sigma_phi, beta_param, tau
> > > > ===== Samplers =====
> > > > RW_block sampler (168)
> > > >   - beta[]  (168 multivariate elements)
> > > > RW sampler (10)
> > > >   - alpha[]  (2 elements)
> > > >   - eta[]  (2 elements)
> > > >   - sigma_phi[]  (2 elements)
> > > >   - beta_param[]  (2 elements)
> > > >   - tau[]  (2 elements)
> > > > CAR_normal sampler (240)
> > > >   - phi_sp[]  (240 multivariate elements)
> > > >    user  system elapsed
> > > >   0.807   0.000   0.805
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > ## code to keep X out of nimble model and vectorize betas -------
> > > > makeRfuns <- function(array_of_matrices) {
> > > >   x <- array_of_matrices
> > > >   RcalcXB <- function(beta) {
> > > >     XB <- array(NA, dim=c(s, t))
> > > >     for(m in 1:t) {
> > > >       for(j in 1:s) {
> > > >         XB[j, m] <- (x[j,1:p,m] %*% beta[j,1:p])[1,1]
> > > >       }
> > > >     }
> > > >     return(XB)
> > > >   }
> > > >   cov_matrix <- function(beta_param) {
> > > >     m <- matrix(NA, 5, 5)
> > > >     diag(m) <- rep(1,5)
> > > >     m[upper.tri(m, diag = FALSE)] <- c(beta_param, beta_param^2, beta_param,
> > > >                                        beta_param^3, beta_param^2, beta_param,
> > > >                                        beta_param^4, beta_param^3, beta_param^2, beta_param)
> > > >     kron <- as.matrix(kronecker(diag(6), forceSymmetric(m)))
> > > >     addrow <- rbind(rep(0,30), kron)
> > > >     return(matrix(cbind(c(1,rep(0,30)), addrow), 31, 31))
> > > >   }
> > > >   list(RcalcXB = RcalcXB, cov_matrix = cov_matrix)
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > # Create the functions and put them in .GlobalEnv
> > > > Rfuns <- makeRfuns(X_array)
> > > > RcalcXB_int <- Rfuns$RcalcXB
> > > > cov_mat_int <- Rfuns$cov_matrix
> > > >
> > > > ## Define the nimbleRcall nimbleFunctions to call the R function
> > > > RcalcXB_model <- nimbleRcall(function(beta = double(2)) {},
> > > >                              returnType = double(2), Rfun = 'RcalcXB_int')
> > > > cov_mat_model <- nimbleRcall(function(beta_param = double()) {},
> > > >                              returnType = double(2), Rfun = 'cov_mat_int')
> > > >
> > > > ## nimble code --------
> > > > ZIPcode_icar <- nimbleCode({
> > > >   # params for mu and pi calculations
> > > >   # i = 2 -> one for mu and one for pi
> > > >   for(i in 1:2) {
> > > >     alpha[i] ~ dnorm(0,5) # scalar intercept params
> > > >     eta[i] ~ dbeta(8,2) # AR param for spatio-temporal adjustments
> > > >     sigma_phi[i] ~ dnorm(0,1)  # time difference spatial sd
> > > >     beta_param[i] ~ dunif(0,1) # AR param for betas
> > > >     tau[i] ~ dnorm(0,5) # precision param
> > > >   }
> > > >
> > > >   # AR(1) on betas - for overfitting (one set of betas for each of 84 regions)
> > > >   zeros[1:p] <- rep(0,p)
> > > >   for(i in 1:2) {
> > > >     cov_matrix[1:p, 1:p, i] <- cov_mat_model(beta_param[i]) * beta_sd
> > > >     for(j in 1:s) {
> > > >       beta[j, 1:p, i] ~ dmnorm(zeros[1:p], cov = cov_matrix[1:p, 1:p, i])
> > > >     }
> > > >   }
> > > >
> > > >   # spatio-temporal effects
> > > >   for(i in 1:2) {
> > > >     phi_sp[1:s, 1, i] ~ dcar_normal(adj = adj[1:L], weights = weights[1:L], num = num[1:s], tau = tau[i])
> > > >     phi_full[1:s, 1, i] <- phi_sp[1:s, 1, i] * sigma_phi[i]
> > > >     for(m in 2:t) {
> > > >       phi_sp[1:s, m, i] ~ dcar_normal(adj = adj[1:L], weights = weights[1:L], num = num[1:s], tau = tau[i])
> > > >       phi_full[1:s, m, i] <- eta[i] * phi_full[1:s, m-1, i]  + phi_sp[1:s, m, i] * sigma_phi[i]
> > > >     }
> > > >   }
> > > >
> > > >   # likelihood params and calculations
> > > >   XB_mu[1:s, 1:t] <- RcalcXB_model(beta[1:s, 1:p, 1])
> > > >   XB_pi[1:s, 1:t] <- RcalcXB_model(beta[1:s, 1:p, 2])
> > > >   for(m in 1:t) {
> > > >     for(j in 1:s) {
> > > >       log(u[j, m]) <- alpha[1] + XB_mu[j, m] + phi_full[j, m, 1] + log_area[j]
> > > >       logit(pi_param[j, m]) <- alpha[2] + XB_pi[j, m] + phi_full[j, m, 2]
> > > >     }
> > > >   }
> > > >
> > > >   # vectorize mu and pi
> > > >   mu[1:(s*t)] <- nimC(u[1:s,1:t])
> > > >   pi[1:(s*t)] <- nimC(pi_param[1:s,1:t])
> > > >
> > > >   for(q in 1:(s*t)) {
> > > >     y[q] ~ dZIP(mu[q], zeroProb = pi[q])
> > > >   }
> > > > })
> > > >
> > > > # define model
> > > > # data, constants, inits
> > > > constants <- list(s = s, p = p, t = t, adj = nbInfo$adj, weights = nbInfo$weights,
> > > >                   num = nbInfo$num, log_area = log_area, L = length(nbInfo$adj), beta_sd = 0.01)
> > > > data <- list(y = y)
> > > > inits <- list(phi_sp = array(matrix(rnorm(s*t, 0, 1), nrow = s, ncol = t), dim = c(s, t, 2)),
> > > >               alpha = c(0.5, 0.5), beta = array(matrix(rnorm(s*p, 0, 1), s,p), dim = c(s,p, 2)),
> > > >               eta = c(0.5, 0.5), beta_param = c(0.5, 0.5), tau = c(0.5, 0.5),
> > > >               sigma_phi = c(0.5, 0.5), cov_matrix = array(matrix(rnorm(p*p, 0, 1), p, p), dim = c(p, p, 2)),
> > > >               zeros = rep(0.5,p)) #,
> > > >               #lifted_chol_oPcov_matrix_oB1to31_comma_1to31_comma_i_cB_cP_L11 = array(matrix(rnorm(p*p, 0, 0.1),p,p), dim = c(2, p,p)))
> > > >
> > > > system.time(ZIP_mod_icar <- nimbleModel(ZIPcode_icar, constants = constants, data = data, inits = inits, calculate = FALSE))
> > > >

messages.body_plain:
Hi Emily

As far as I am aware nimble uses the WAIC only for goodness of fit.

This is a more stable improvement of DIC.

If you want the DIC you would need to compute the deviance within the program

and compute your on pD. The simplest way would be to use the conservative

pD estimate of (sd(deviance)**2)/2 . The sd(deviance)  is available from the sample summary

if you computed the deviance in the code.

Hope this is useful.

best

Andrew

messages.body_plain:
Hi Emily,

Actually there's an easier way to do this than writing out the
calculation yourself. You can monitor logProb values for one or more
variables.

It would look something like this (if the variable of interest were
'mu' and you wanted to monitor it and its log density):

mcmc=configureMCMC(model, monitors=c('mu','logProb_mu'))

(There are also other ways to specify what is monitored, but that is
one standard way.)

So if you only need to calculate the deviance, you should be able to
monitor the relevant logProb and then use that after the sampling is
complete.

There is also a post to this list from June 21 titled "storing sums of
log probabilities" that discusses how to monitor the logProb of
multiple variables all at once. I think you don't need that, but just
noting it in case of use.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,
Just a quick follow-up on the different solution I tested following Perry and Daniel advices:

- For following the adaptation phase of the slice sampler, I tested the manual solution of stopping the mcmc every 200 runs but it is quite time consuming to run through numerous samplers each time to get the `width` (it is still running in fact). I may test at some point the implementation I proposed in the dev version of nimble, but did not have time for it yet.

- I also did some test by fixing the scale of the different RW samplers involved in the problematic nodes. Nothing conclusive for now. But I was wondering if it would be possible to use non-adaptive RW and still follow acceptance rate  ?

Best,
Rémi

On Friday, July 31, 2020 at 5:04:21 PM UTC+2 pdevalpine wrote:
> Hi Rémi,
>
> Sure that makes sense.  You could write a for loop to iterate over samplers for many nodes to set the proposal scale and turn the adapt flag FALSE for each one.  I suggested it because it sounded like you were conjecturing that the adaptation has not resulted in proposal scales that you think are most efficient.  (We usually think of efficiency in terms of (effective sample size) / computation time.  The computation time shouldn't change much or at all for different proposal scales, but the effective sample sizes almost certainly will.)  That is possible.  If you increase proposal scale, it may or may not increase effective sample size.  If it does, then fewer iterations would be needed.  I hope that helps.  Let us know if you get interesting results.
>
> -Perry
>
> On Fri, Jul 31, 2020 at 7:48 AM Rémi PATIN <remi....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi Perry,
> > Thank you for the suggestion and the explanations to do it, I will give it a try. I am however a bit afraid to fix the RW proposal scale, because it concerns around ~2000 nodes. So I am not sure whether a single (or even a few) scale for all the nodes could do the trick.
> > I suppose if I manually fix the scale to higher value than produced by the adaptation phase, acceptation rate for those nodes will drop leading to slower iteration through those nodes. Meanwhile the samples should be less autocorrelated and less iterations would be needed ?
> >
> > Concerning initial values, the model should have relatively good ones for most nodes. I know they have already worked on that and I think that we are currently using older model outputs to initiate the nodes in question. But I will keep that in mind, this could still be problematic.
> >
> > Best,
> > Rémi
> >
> > Le vendredi 31 juillet 2020 16:18:06 UTC+2, pdevalpine a écrit :
> > > Hi Rémi,
> > >
> > > If you think the RW proposal scale has adapted to a value that is too small, I can give three suggestions for exploring the issue.
> > >
> > > 1. At the stage of the MCMC configuration (after configureMCMC) but before building the MCMC (before buildMCMC), find the relevant sampler by inspection of mcmcConf$printSamplers() or mcmcConf$getSamplers().  (Here mcmcConf is the object returned by configureMCMC).  Then modify the control list of that sampler to have adapt=FALSE and scale=<your choice>.
> > >
> > > 2. You can make the same settings by modifying the MCMC (after buildMCMC).  If you do it in the uncompiled version (before compileNimble), you can modify mcmc$samplerFunctions[[idx]]$scale and mcmc$samplerFunctions[[idx]]$adapt, where mcmc is the uncompiled MCMC.  Those values will then be copied to the compiled version to initialize it during compileNimble.  If you want to do it after compileNimble (with say Cmcmc instead of mcmc, where Cmcmc is the compiled version), you will need the same nimbleOptions setting Daniel provided.  You may want to do it this way because you could run it for a while, look at the scale value, then manually adjust it and continue running (with reset = FALSE) to experiment.
> > >
> > > 3. Sometimes providing good initial values can improve the outcome of the RW adaptation.  If the initial values are far from the main posterior region, then much of the adaptation can occur during updates that are just finding the main posterior region, which can behave very differently that updates in the main region.
> > >
> > > HTH
> > > -Perry
> > >
> > >
> > > On Fri, Jul 31, 2020 at 6:51 AM Daniel Turek <db...@williams.edu> wrote:
> > > > Good question, Rémi.  And I'm glad to hear you found the diagnostic information (scaleHistory, acceptanceRateHistory, etc) in the RW sampler to be helpful.
> > > >
> > > > At present, there's no such facilities in the slice sampler to record this history of the adaption process.  The slice sampler does adapt (every adaptInterval MCMC iterations), to modify the internal "width" variable, to make this "extension" width of the horizontal slice more suitable for the scale of the posterior distribution.  So, yes, tracking this "widthHistory" would be analogous to the adaptation history information in the RW sampler.
> > > >
> > > > At present, this information is not tracked in the slice sampler, but similar methods "getWidthHistory" could be added to the slice sampler.  I don't believe there are plans for adding it at the moment, but we would certainly welcome (and review) a pull-request to add this to the system.
> > > >
> > > > Short of that, modifying the sampler code and/or the nimble code base, you could also track this "width history" by extracting the "width" variable from the slice sampler after each MCMC iteration, making sure to set the nimble option:
> > > > nimbleOptions(buildInterfacesForCompiledNestedNimbleFunctions = TRUE)
> > > >
> > > > This would work fine, and accomplish your goals.  A short example showing how to do that is below.
> > > >
> > > > Good luck with this,
> > > > Daniel
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > library(nimble)
> > > > nimbleOptions(buildInterfacesForCompiledNestedNimbleFunctions = TRUE)
> > > >
> > > > code <- nimbleCode({
> > > >     a ~ dnorm(0, 1)
> > > > })
> > > > constants <- list()
> > > > data <- list()
> > > > inits <- list(a = 0)
> > > >
> > > > Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code, constants, data, inits)
> > > > Rmodel$calculate()
> > > >
> > > > conf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, nodes = NULL)
> > > > conf$addSampler('a', 'slice')
> > > >
> > > > Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(conf)
> > > >
> > > > Cmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
> > > > Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Rmodel)
> > > >
> > > > niter <- 10000
> > > > set.seed(0)
> > > > widthHistory <- numeric(niter)
> > > >
> > > > for(i in 1:niter) {
> > > >     Cmcmc$run(1, reset = (i==1))
> > > >     widthHistory[i] <- Cmcmc$samplerFunctions[[1]]$width
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > samples <- as.matrix(Cmcmc$mvSamples)
> > > >
> > > > plot(1:niter, widthHistory, type = 'l')
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Fri, Jul 31, 2020 at 2:27 AM Rémi PATIN <remi...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > Hi all,
> > > > > I have seen that you can follow the adaptation process of the RW sampler by using
> > > > > cmcmc$samplerFunctions[[idx]]$getScaleHistory()
> > > > >
> > > > > and
> > > > > cmcmc$samplerFunctions[[idx]]$getAcceptanceHistory()
> > > > >
> > > > > I suppose it is not yet possible (but maybe scheduled at some point?) to get similar information for other samplers such as slice for instance ?
> > > > >
> > > > > I have some nodes for which the RW adaptation decreases greatly the scale to keep acceptance rate high enough, which produces some highly autocorrelated samples. So I wanted to try other samplers (currently the slice) to see if it could ease the process and I was curious to see if there was a similar process during the adapatation phase for the slice samplers (but maybe you would have other suggestions for such cases).
> > > > >
> > > > > Thanks in advance,
> > > > > Rémi
